title: Communicate verbally with clients in a financial environment

lessons.title: Preparing to speak with clients
lessons.html:
Why verbal communication matters

At a silo office, grain cooperative or agribusiness, many client conversations are about money: payments for delivered grain, storage charges, grading deductions, credit and contract prices. Farmers make important business decisions on what you tell them. A misunderstanding can cost a client thousands of rand and damage the relationship with the business. Good verbal communication is therefore a core skill, not a nice extra.

Know your clients

Clients include commercial grain producers, emerging and smallholder farmers, buyers such as millers and feedlots, transport contractors and agents acting for clients. They speak different home languages and have different levels of financial experience. Adapt to the person in front of you. Where possible and allowed, use the client's preferred language or arrange someone who can help.

Prepare before the conversation

  • For a planned call or meeting, have the client's account, recent transactions and relevant documents ready.
  • Know the current tariffs, payment dates and procedures that apply.
  • Decide the main points you need to get across.
  • Find a quiet place. Noise from the intake or weighbridge makes phone calls difficult.

Professional standards

Your organisation will have standards for greeting clients, answering the phone and dressing. Follow them. Always identify yourself and the business, and verify the client before discussing account details. Be aware that financial advice may only be given by persons authorised to do so under the Financial Advisory and Intermediary Services Act 37 of 2002 (FAIS). If you are not authorised, give factual information only and refer the client.

lessons.title: Speaking and listening effectively
lessons.html:
Active listening

Good communication starts with listening. Active listening means giving the client your full attention and showing that you understand.

  • Let the client finish speaking before you respond.
  • Make notes of key facts: amounts, dates, reference numbers.
  • Use short responses such as "I understand" or "Yes, go on" to show you are following.
  • Ask open questions to get more detail, for example "What happened when the truck was weighed?"
  • Ask closed questions to confirm facts, for example "Is your client number 4521?"
  • Summarise: "So you delivered 32 tons on Monday and you expected payment on Friday. Is that right?"

Speaking clearly

  • Use plain language. Instead of "the net realisation after deductions", say "the amount you receive after the drying and handling charges are taken off".
  • Speak at a steady pace and pronounce numbers carefully. Repeat important figures, and spell out reference numbers.
  • Check understanding: "Does that make sense?" or "Would you like me to go through the charges again?"
  • Keep your tone calm, polite and confident.

On the telephone

On the phone the client cannot see your face, so your voice carries everything. Smile when you speak; it changes your tone. Do not eat or chew while on a call. If you need to put the client on hold, ask permission and come back regularly. If you must call back, agree a time and keep to it.

Non-verbal communication in person

Face the client, make appropriate eye contact, and keep an open posture. Avoid looking at your phone. Respect cultural differences in greetings and personal space.

lessons.title: Handling difficult conversations and complaints
lessons.html:
When clients are upset

A farmer whose payment is late, or whose maize was downgraded, may be angry. Often the anger is about pressure they are under: paying workers, buying inputs or repaying a production loan. Your job is to stay professional and help solve the problem.

A simple approach

  1. Listen without interrupting. Let the client explain fully.
  2. Acknowledge the feeling: "I can hear this delay is causing you real problems."
  3. Clarify the facts with questions and check the records.
  4. Explain what has happened in plain language, without blaming colleagues or the client.
  5. Agree on the next step and a time frame.
  6. Follow up and do what you promised.

What not to do

  • Do not argue or raise your voice.
  • Do not make promises you cannot keep, such as guaranteeing a payment date you do not control.
  • Do not give out another client's information to make a point.
  • Do not take it personally.

If a client becomes abusive or threatening, stay calm, end the conversation politely if needed and inform your supervisor.

Escalating

Know your organisation's complaints procedure. Some matters, such as grading disputes or requests for fee waivers, must be referred to a supervisor or specialist. When you escalate, give the full details so the client does not have to repeat the story.

Recording the conversation

After important conversations, record the date, who you spoke to, what was discussed, what was agreed and any follow-up. Clear records support consistent service and protect both the client and the business.

Key points

  • Prepare with the client's records and current tariffs before important conversations.
  • Verify the client and give only factual information unless you are authorised to advise.
  • Listen actively, summarise and check understanding.
  • Use plain language and repeat important figures carefully.
  • With complaints: listen, acknowledge, clarify, explain, agree and follow up.

quiz.question: Which law governs who may give financial advice?

options.text: Conservation of Agricultural Resources Act 43 of 1983
Financial Advisory and Intermediary Services Act 37 of 2002

quiz.question: Which is an example of summarising?

options.text: So you delivered 32 tons on Monday and expected payment on Friday. Is that right?
What is the weather like on your farm?
The amount you receive after the drying and handling charges are taken off

quiz.question: A client is angry about a late payment. What should you do first?

options.text: Explain that it is not your fault

quiz.question: Why should you repeat important figures and spell out reference numbers?

options.text: To avoid misunderstandings about amounts and references

quiz.question: It is acceptable to guarantee a payment date you do not control if it calms the client down.
On the telephone your tone of voice carries most of your message because the client cannot see you.
Which are signs of active listening? (select all that apply)

options.text: Letting the client finish before responding
Making notes of amounts and dates
Checking your phone while the client talks
